newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy replaces secret service chiefs.
newsitem.headline: Italy replaces secret service chiefs.

text.p: Italy's centre-left government replaced the heads of the country's secret service agencies on Friday in a move that raised protests from the opposition.

An official statement said the change at the top of the intelligence tree was connected to a planned reform of the secret services, never far from controversy in a country where plots real or imagined surface regularly.

Vittorio Stelo, the prefect or chief law and order official in Turin, was named to head the civilian intelligence service SISDE with an admiral, Gianfranco Battelli, appointed to the military intelligence agency SISMI.
Leadership of CESIS, an umbrella body meant to monitor and coordinate the work of the two services, was also changed, with Florence prefect Francesco Berardino named secretary general.
The new men replace heads of the three bodies who were appointed just two years ago by the centre-right government led by media magnate Silvio Berlusconi.
His opposition Freedom Alliance criticised the changes as an act of arrogance by the "Olive Tree" coalition government of Prime Minister Romano Prodi, which was appointed last May.
"You really get the impression that the Olive Tree is desperately trying to occupy everything before it is too late," centre-right political Pier Ferdinando Casini said.
Another Berlusconi ally, hard right politician Maurizio Gasparri, said the government had given preference to "the systematic occupation of power over a calm and serious study of the problems".

The criticisms were rejected by the government, which said the appointments were linked only to the planned intelligence overhaul aimed at what the statement said was a "clear definition and distribution of duties between the services".
"I don't understand why the Freedom Alliance is worried about these changes," Deputy Prime Minister Walter Veltroni said.
He said the switch was not connected to a political storm over the past week since Berlusconi announced that he had discovered a bugging device in his Rome office.
Interior Minister Giorgio Napolitano, who has political control of SISDE, told parliament this week that there was no evidence secret service agents were involved in the eavesdropping.
So-called "deviant offshoots" of Italy's intelligence agencies have long been suspected of working to their own agenda or to the instructions of political barons.
Allegations that spies had a hand in some of the extremist bombings which destabilised Italy in the 1970s and in other unresolved mysteries of the past 30 years have never been fully laid to rest.
